title: Level 9: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Conversion) via Polling
aim: To configure the ATmega328P's 10-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) to read the analog voltage output of a potentiometer connected to ADC0 (PC0) and display the result by proportionally controlling LED brightness via PWM.
objective: Understand the ADC hardware module (ADMUX, ADCSRA registers), the ADC clock prescaler requirement, conversion triggering and result reading, and mapping 10-bit ADC values to PWM duty cycles.
theory:
What is an ADC?

The physical world is analog — voltages vary continuously from 0 to 5 V. Microcontrollers are digital — they only understand 0 and 1. An Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) bridges this gap by sampling an analog voltage and converting it to a discrete integer value. The ATmega328P has a built-in 10-bit, 6-channel ADC on Port C pins (ADC0–ADC5, PC0–PC5).

10-Bit Resolution

With a 10-bit ADC, the input voltage range (0 to VREF) is divided into 2^10 = 1024 discrete steps. The ADC result formula:

ADC_result = (V_in / V_ref) × 1023

With VREF = VCC = 5 V: 0 V → 0, 2.5 V → 511, 5 V → 1023. The resolution is 5/1023 ≈ 4.88 mV per step.

The Potentiometer as a Voltage Divider

A potentiometer is a variable voltage divider. It has three terminals: two outer terminals connected across the power supply (GND and VCC), and a centre wiper that slides from one end to the other. The wiper voltage varies linearly from 0 V to 5 V as the knob is turned — a perfect analog input source for ADC testing.

ADMUX — ADC Multiplexer Select Register

  • REFS1:REFS0 (bits 7:6) — Voltage reference selection. REFS1=0, REFS0=1 → use AVCC (VCC = 5 V) as reference
  • ADLAR (bit 5) — Result alignment. 0 = Right-adjusted (standard, use ADCL+ADCH for 10-bit). 1 = Left-adjusted (only need ADCH for 8-bit)
  • MUX3:MUX0 (bits 3:0) — Input channel select. 0000 = ADC0, 0001 = ADC1, ..., 0101 = ADC5

ADCSRA — ADC Control and Status Register A

  • ADEN (bit 7) — ADC Enable. Must be 1 to power on the ADC module
  • ADSC (bit 6) — ADC Start Conversion. Write 1 to begin a conversion; hardware clears it when done
  • ADATE (bit 5) — Auto Trigger Enable (for continuous/free-running mode)
  • ADIF (bit 4) — ADC Interrupt Flag (set when conversion completes)
  • ADIE (bit 3) — ADC Interrupt Enable
  • ADPS2:ADPS0 (bits 2:0) — ADC Clock Prescaler. ADC requires 50–200 kHz clock. At 16 MHz, set prescaler to ÷128 → 125 kHz ADC clock

Polling Conversion

In polling mode: write ADSC=1 to start conversion, then loop until ADSC becomes 0 (hardware clears it on completion). Read ADCL then ADCH (low byte first is mandatory for correct 10-bit result): result = ADCL | (ADCH << 8);

Mapping ADC to PWM

The 10-bit result (0–1023) must be mapped to the 8-bit PWM duty cycle register OCR0A (0–255): OCR0A = ADC_result / 4; (dividing by 4 scales 0–1023 to 0–255).

pretest.question: What is the resolution of the ATmega328P's ADC in bits?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P has a 10-bit ADC giving 2^10 = 1024 discrete output values (0–1023).

pretest.question: With VREF = 5 V and a 10-bit ADC, what is the voltage at ADC result = 512?
pretest.explanation: V_in = (512 / 1023) × 5 V ≈ 2.5 V. ADC result 512 corresponds to approximately mid-scale voltage.

pretest.question: Which register selects the ADC input channel and voltage reference?
pretest.explanation: ADMUX (ADC Multiplexer Selection Register) holds REFS1:REFS0 (voltage reference) and MUX3:MUX0 (channel selection).

pretest.question: What REFS setting selects AVCC (5V) as the ADC voltage reference?
pretest.explanation: REFS1=0, REFS0=1 in ADMUX selects AVCC as the ADC reference voltage, making the full-scale ADC input equal to VCC (typically 5 V).

pretest.question: What must be done before an ADC conversion can complete?
pretest.explanation: Writing ADSC=1 (ADC Start Conversion bit) in ADCSRA triggers a single conversion. Hardware clears this bit when the result is ready.

pretest.question: Why is an ADC clock prescaler of ÷128 used at 16 MHz?
options: ADC requires 50–200 kHz input clock; 16MHz/128 = 125 kHz falls within this range
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P ADC achieves maximum accuracy with a clock between 50 kHz and 200 kHz. At 16 MHz, ADPS2:ADPS0 = 111 (÷128) gives 125 kHz.

pretest.question: Why must you read ADCL before ADCH?
options: Reading ADCL first locks the 16-bit register pair; subsequent ADCH read gives the correct upper bits
ADCL and ADCH can be read in any order
pretest.explanation: The AVR locks the ADCH register when ADCL is read, preventing corruption if a new conversion completes between reads. Always read ADCL first.

pretest.question: How do you map a 10-bit ADC value (0–1023) to an 8-bit PWM register (0–255)?
pretest.explanation: 1023 / 4 ≈ 255. Dividing by 4 (right-shifting by 2 bits) scales 10-bit ADC to 8-bit PWM range. For exact mapping: OCR0A = ADC >> 2.

pretest.question: What does a potentiometer wiper do?
options: Provides a variable voltage tap between 0V and VCC proportional to position
pretest.explanation: The wiper slides along a resistive track, forming a voltage divider. As it moves from one end to the other, its voltage linearly goes from 0 V to VCC.

pretest.question: How many ADC channels does the ATmega328P have?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P has 6 ADC channels (ADC0–ADC5) mapped to Port C pins PC0–PC5 (Arduino A0–A5). The ADMUX MUX bits select among them.

procedure: Include #include <avr/io.h>. Define #define F_CPU 16000000UL. Wire the potentiometer: left terminal → GND, right terminal → 5V, wiper (centre) → PC0 (Arduino A0 = ADC0). Wire LED with 330 Ω to Pin 6 (PD6 = OC0A) for PWM brightness.

Configure the PWM output first: set DDRD bit 6 as output, set TCCR0A for Fast PWM non-inverting on OC0A, set TCCR0B for ÷8 prescaler: DDRD |= (1<<PD6); TCCR0A=(1<<COM0A1)|(1<<WGM01)|(1<<WGM00); TCCR0B=(1<<CS01);
Configure the ADC reference voltage to AVCC and select channel ADC0 (MUX = 0000) in ADMUX: ADMUX = (1 << REFS0);. REFS0=1, MUX bits = 0000 → AVCC reference, ADC0 channel.
Configure ADCSRA: enable the ADC (ADEN=1) and set the ADC prescaler to ÷128 (ADPS2=1, ADPS1=1, ADPS0=1) for 125 kHz ADC clock: ADCSRA = (1<<ADEN)|(1<<ADPS2)|(1<<ADPS1)|(1<<ADPS0);
Perform a dummy first conversion and discard the result — the first ADC conversion after enabling has reduced accuracy: ADCSRA |= (1<<ADSC); while(ADCSRA & (1<<ADSC)); (void)ADC;
In the main loop, start a conversion: ADCSRA |= (1 << ADSC);. Poll (busy-wait) until the ADSC bit clears: while(ADCSRA & (1 << ADSC));.
Read the 10-bit result: uint16_t adcValue = ADC;. The AVR C runtime handles reading ADCL then ADCH correctly when you use the ADC macro.
Map to PWM: OCR0A = adcValue >> 2; (right-shift by 2 = divide by 4, scaling 0–1023 to 0–255). Rotate the potentiometer and observe the LED brightness change smoothly proportional to the pot position.

posttest.question: What is the ADC result when the input voltage is exactly 3.3 V with VREF = 5 V?
What is the voltage resolution (minimum detectable change) of the 10-bit ADC at 5V reference?
posttest.explanation: Resolution = VREF / 1023 = 5 / 1023 ≈ 4.88 mV per LSB (Least Significant Bit).

posttest.question: What is 'free-running' ADC mode?
options: ADC automatically starts a new conversion immediately after each completes
posttest.explanation: Setting ADATE=1 and ADTS=0 in ADCSRB enables free-running mode: conversions happen continuously at full speed, with ADIF flag set after each.

posttest.question: What causes ADC noise and how can it be reduced?
options: Coupling from GPIO switching — use ADC Noise Reduction sleep mode and AVCC decoupling capacitor
posttest.explanation: Digital switching on GPIO and power supply noise couple into the analog domain. Solutions: 100 nF decoupling caps on AVCC/AREF, use ADC Noise Reduction sleep mode, and add analog input RC filter.

posttest.question: What is the internal 1.1V bandgap reference useful for?
options: Accurate measurements independent of VCC fluctuations
posttest.explanation: The ATmega328P has an internal 1.1V bandgap reference (REFS = 11). Since it's fixed and independent of VCC, it's more stable for precision measurements when VCC fluctuates.

posttest.question: Why would you use interrupt-driven ADC instead of polling?
options: The CPU is free to do other tasks while waiting for the ~104 µs conversion time
posttest.explanation: A 10-bit conversion takes 13 ADC clock cycles (÷128 = 125 kHz → 104 µs). Polling wastes this time. ADIE interrupt lets the CPU sleep or handle other tasks.

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: The WDT auto-resets the MCU if not periodically cleared — essential for field reliability.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has Port B, C, D only.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile memory — all contents lost on power-off.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: AVR hardware clears the I-bit in SREG on ISR entry.

feedback: Excellent! The ADC is your MCU's window to the physical world. Every sensor — temperature, light, pressure, sound — ultimately outputs an analog voltage that an ADC converts to usable digital data. You've mastered this critical interface.
